claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Cu HEA coating containing 20 at.% of each element on an SS-304 substrate.
The as-deposited HEA has no pre-formed protective oxide film.
Mechanical sliding and exposure to a corrosive medium are to be applied concurrently.
An oxidative environment at elevated temperature promotes spinel-oxide formation in the Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Cu coating.
A high-entropy (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4 spinel forms in situ by thermal oxidation.
The in-situ high-entropy spinel forms a continuous film.
Sliding cyclically removes and reforms portions of the high-entropy spinel film.
The spinel layer resists wear because of its inherent hardness.
The spinel layer protects against corrosion by acting as a passivating barrier.
Fresh alloy exposed by removal of the oxide rapidly re-oxidizes into the same spinel.
The balance between oxide removal and reformation governs both mechanical damage and corrosive attack.
Relative to a baseline with suppressed spinel formation, the spinel-forming alloy will exhibit lower total degradation.
Relative to the baseline, the spinel-forming alloy will exhibit reduced wear depth.
Relative to the baseline, the spinel-forming alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current.
The simultaneous wear and corrosion improvements constitute a synergistic increase in durability.
The control is a matched HEA processed or modified to suppress formation of the high-entropy spinel.
The prediction should hold when oxidation is sufficient for meaningful oxide reformation and wear is moderate.
The protection may fail when wear removes the oxide faster than it reforms or when the environment is inert.
Oxide-film reformation kinetics and the effects of microstructural heterogeneity on film adhesion and integrity are uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both wear and corrosion, or failure to observe dynamic oxide removal and reformation, would falsify the hypothesis.
